slot.brief: A block slides from rest down a curved frictionless track onto a rough horizontal stretch; use energy conservation plus work-energy theorem to find where it stops.

stem: A block starts from rest and descends through a vertical height of $5$ m along a frictionless curved track. It then crosses a horizontal rough stretch whose first $4$ m has coefficient of friction $0.25$, followed by a portion with coefficient $0.5$. Taking $g=10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, how far from the start of the rough stretch does it stop?

verdicts.working: The block reaches the rough stretch with 50 J/kg of kinetic energy. The first 4 m dissipates 0.25×10×4 = 10 J/kg, leaving 40 J/kg. At μ = 0.5, friction dissipates 5 J/kg per metre, so it travels 8 m further. Total distance = 12 m.

working:
Energy per unit mass at entry: $gh=50$ J kg$^{-1}$.
Work per unit mass over first $4$ m: $0.25(10)(4)=10$ J kg$^{-1}$.
Remaining energy: $40$ J kg$^{-1}$; distance in second portion $=40/[0.5(10)]=8$ m.
Total distance $=4+8=12$ m.

Independent check: The block reaches the rough stretch with 50 J/kg of kinetic energy. The first 4 m dissipates 0.25×10×4 = 10 J/kg, leaving 40 J/kg. At μ = 0.5, friction dissipates 5 J/kg per metre, so it travels 8 m further. Total distance = 12 m.
solution:
By conservation of energy, the kinetic energy per unit mass at the rough stretch is $gh=10(5)=50\,\text{J kg}^{-1}$. The first $4$ m dissipates $\mu g d=0.25(10)(4)=10\,\text{J kg}^{-1}$, leaving $40\,\text{J kg}^{-1}$.
$$d_2=\frac{40}{0.5(10)}=8\,\text{m},\qquad d=4+8=12\,\text{m}.$$
